title: Database Replication
sources: Kleppmann, Designing Data-Intensive Applications, ch. 5 'Replication': replication means keeping a copy of the same data on multiple machines connected by a network, to keep the system working if parts fail, to scale out reads, and to reduce latency

DDIA ch. 5 'Leaders and Followers' (single-leader / primary-replica): clients send writes to the leader, which sends each data change to all followers; reads can be served by the leader or any follower
DDIA ch. 5 'Handling Node Outages: Leader failover': if the leader fails, one of the followers is promoted to be the new leader and clients send writes to it

DDIA ch. 5 'Problems with Replication Lag' and DesignGurus 'Database replication': with asynchronous replication a follower can fall behind, so a read from it may briefly return outdated data (eventual consistency)

lines.text: Yesterday we made finding orders instant,
but all ten million live on one database.
If that one machine dies, every order is gone.
Replication fixes that, by keeping copies.
Think of a head chef with the master order book,
lines.caps: *THINK OF | A HEAD *CHEF | WITH THE *MASTER | ORDER *BOOK

lines.text: and every new order gets copied into the other cooks' books.
lines.caps: AND EVERY *NEW | *ORDER | GETS *COPIED | INTO THE *OTHER | COOKS' *BOOKS

lines.text: In databases, the leader takes all the writes,
and the followers copy every change.
Now reads can go to any copy,
so way more people get served at once.
a follower gets promoted and takes over.
The catch? A copy can lag a moment behind.
One database is a gamble. Copies are insurance.
